Measured blow times differ from the declared curve by up to 233%, faster than the datasheet. Faster than published is safer for the wire and worse for nuisance trips; re-check inrush. Counterfeit or mislabelled blade fuses are common enough that this is the expected explanation, not an exotic one.

Measured blow times differ from the declared curve by up to 160%, SLOWER than the datasheet. A fuse slower than its published curve invalidates every coordination result computed from that curve — the wire protection you signed off does not exist. Counterfeit or mislabelled blade fuses are common enough that this is the expected explanation, not an exotic one.

No declared fuse curve, so the expected blow times are unknown and the plan cannot say which points the rig can resolve. Testing blind is still possible — but start at 2x rating and work up, because a point that clears faster than the rig can see returns a number that looks fine.

Sized on an ASSUMED spread (sigma_ln = 0.30, module prior (not your fuses)), which nothing here has verified for the parts in your drawer. The count is quadratic in that assumption: if your fuses scatter half again as widely, this becomes 24 per level rather than 11. Run five at one current, pass them to refine_from_pilot(), and this stops being a guess.

2 current levels x 11 samples = 22 fuses (about 33 at 1.50 each) to pin the median blow time to ±20% at each level. 11 per level comes from the log-normal scatter of blow times, not from a round number — one fuse per level is an anecdote.

2 of 4 planned points are below what this rig can resolve (5x → 160.0 ms, 10x → 40.0 ms). Those are the short-circuit points — the ones that decide whether the harness survives — so a rig that can only take the slow points measures the region that matters least.
proof-of-concept (operator keypress, millis): timer resolution 1000 us, detection latency 281.2 ms, combined uncertainty ±80.0 ms. Shortest event measurable to 10% is 800 ms.

Blocking serial output sits between the start and stop marks: 30 characters at 9600 baud is 31 ms added to every reading, in one direction only. Buffer the results and print after the test, not during it.

Blow detection is manual, so the 281 ms in this measurement is the operator's reaction time and not a property of the fuse. Every reading is biased long by roughly that much, and the bias is larger than most of the blow times worth measuring. Detect the current collapse on a shunt instead.
An expected blow time of 40.0 ms is noise, not a measurement: ±80.0 ms is 200% of it. Resolving this point to 5% needs detection at 500 Hz or faster.
